_note: The Turn — doors distilled from the retrieved Catena Aurea (Newman tr.), verified line-by-line against ~/reception-corpus. Editorial framing AI-drafted, status:draft, pending Wilson's curation.
gravity: Israel marks the Passover with blood on the doorposts, the sign that turns death aside (Exodus 12); Paul reduces the whole law to one debt that's never paid off — "owe no one anything, except to love one another" (Romans 13); and Jesus gives a specific procedure for confronting sin in the community — private first, then witnesses, then the whole church. The nerve: love for the offender, not exposure of the offender, drives every step of the process.
trap: Becomes a weapon (church discipline as public shaming, or a rulebook for cutting someone off) or is avoided altogether ("just forgive and forget," skip the confrontation) — missing that the goal named at each step is to *gain* the brother, not to win an argument.
hinge: The process ends in a possible verdict of "let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector" — yet Jesus spent his whole ministry eating with Gentiles and tax collectors. The most severe thing this text allows is: treat him like someone I would still go find.

doors.claim: Confrontation begins one-on-one, in private, because shame compounds sin rather than curing it.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Thy brother is to be reproved in private, lest if once he has lost a sense of shame, he should continue in sin.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Our Lord admonishes us not to overlook one another's faults, yet not so as seeking for matter of blame, but watching what you may amend.

doors.say: The first move is never public — not because sin should be hidden, but because shame, once a person loses it, stops correcting anything.
doors.do: Ask them to name someone they're tempted to expose rather than approach, and go to that person alone first.

doors.claim: Reconciliation is a gain for both people, not a victory for one — the goal reframes confrontation as rescue, not conquest.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He said not, he has gained himself, but, you have gained him; which shews that both of you are the gainers.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: For in saving another, salvation is gained for ourselves also.

doors.say: When you go to confront someone, you're not just trying to fix them — you're trying to get both of you back.
doors.do: Have them reframe one grievance they're holding as a potential mutual gain, not a case to win.

doors.landing: Like a Gentile and a tax collector
doors.claim: The harshest verdict this text allows is to treat someone the way Jesus treated Gentiles and tax collectors — which is to say, still pursued, still eaten with, never written off.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: That He says, 'As a heathen and a publican,' shews that he is to be more abhorred, who under the name of a believer does the deeds of an unbeliever.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Though even thus we are not to neglect his salvation; for the heathens themselves, that is, the gentiles...

doors.say: Even the worst verdict in this text isn't exile — it's the status Jesus spent his whole ministry crossing over to reach.
doors.do: Ask them to name someone they've functionally written off, and identify one way Jesus would still be pursuing that person.

subtract: Three landings — the private first step, the mutual gain, or what the harshest verdict actually permits. Choose one and let the others go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.

synthesis.convergence: Passover blood marks a door so death passes over, not so the household is exposed (Exodus 12); Paul reduces every commandment to one unpaid debt — love (Romans 13); and Jesus' whole procedure for confronting sin aims at gathering back in, ending in the promise that where two or three gather in his name, he is there. Every reading refuses a religion of exposure for a religion of restoration.
synthesis.claim: The point of naming what's wrong is never exposure — it's the door left open for someone to come back through.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that either weaponizes accountability or avoids it entirely, name the actual goal Jesus gives: not being right, not being safe from confrontation, but gaining each other back.
